description_full: Snap-on Incorporated manufactures and markets tools, equipment, diagnostics, and repair information and systems solutions for professional users worldwide. It operates through Commercial & Industrial Group, Snap-on Tools Group, Repair Systems & Information Group, and Financial Services segments. The company offers hand tools, such as wrenches, sockets, ratchet wrenches, pliers, screwdrivers, punches and chisels, saws and cutting tools, pruning tools, torque tools, and other similar products; power tools, including cordless, pneumatic, and hydraulic and corded tools; impact wrenches, ratchets, screwdrivers, drills, sanders, and grinders. It also provides tool chests and roll cabinet stool storage products; facility-level tool control and asset management hardware and software; diagnostics, information, and management systems product comprising handheld and computer-based diagnostic products, service and repair information products, diagnostic software solutions, electronic parts catalogs, business management systems and services, point-of-sale systems, integrated systems for vehicle service shops, OEM purchasing facilitation services, and warranty management systems and analytics to help OEM dealerships manage and track performance. In addition, the company offers wheel alignment equipment, wheel balancers, tire changers, vehicle lifts, test lane equipment, collision repair equipment, vehicle air conditioning service equipment, brake service equipment, fluid exchange equipment, transmission troubleshooting equipment, safety testing equipment, battery chargers, and hoists; and training programs and after-sales support. It serves the vehicle service and repair, and industrial sectors through mobile van channel, company direct sales, distributors, and digital commerce. In addition, it distributes and services vehicle collision equipment in Australia. Snap-on Incorporated was incorporated in 1920 and is based in Kenosha, Wisconsin.
ceo_bio: Mr. Nicholas T. Pinchuk | Chairman, CEO & President | Age 78 | Compensation: $2.1M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 13K people. Revenue per employee of $397K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $77K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Snap-On Incorporated is a large-cap industrials business with a $18.9B market cap on $5.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 8% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.06× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 26× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.4% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Above-average short interest at 8.4% of float
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $23.5M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 8% over 3 months
Industrials ETF trading well below its long-term trend
Cyclical sectors like Industrials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 8% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Operating margins 17% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
40 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible

sect: Its 26% operating margin runs 17pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.34x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 11% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.12 vs 5y 0.72), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $106.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 15% in the 2022 bear market and 66% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $412, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $334 to $523 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 64% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $404 on average, 10% above the price.
The price implies 3.0% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 8.3% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.06x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $438.1M (2% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.1% over 3 years, 5.5% over 5 years and 3.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 42% of profits supports about 8.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (1.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.4%, and institutions hold 100%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (29 sales, net $23.5M sold).
It returns 4.2% a year to shareholders (1.7% in buybacks and 2.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 13.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 13,000 employees, each generates about $397K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.5% a year.
That works out to $77K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
